cues.text: We now move into a set of submitted continuous assessment questions, worked as revision.
Before we begin, two cautions from the source.
Original archived options are retained wherever they were captured.
The answer key here is provisional, not official.
And some photographed question stems were paraphrased during transcription, so treat the wording with that in mind.
Let us start with CA Question 7.
A project uses sign-offs at every stage, but stakeholders approve requirements without reading them.
What quality risk remains?
There are four options.
Option A: sign-offs function as ceremonial rather than meaningful controls.
Option B: requirements become automatically correct upon signing off.
Option C: sign-offs eliminate the need for validation.
Option D: testing processes should be cancelled entirely if signed.
The provisional reviewed answer is A.
The reasoning is that formal approval is ineffective when stakeholders do not perform substantive review.
A signature is only a control if someone has actually examined what they are signing.
If nobody reads the requirements, the sign-off becomes a ceremony, and the quality risk stays exactly where it was.
Options B, C and D each assume the signature itself guarantees correctness, which is the very assumption this scenario undermines.
On to CA Question 8.
In the Spiral model, a defence software company has completed detailed risk assessment of cybersecurity and integration threats.
What comes next?
Option A: engineering, prototyping, and other core development activities follow.
Option B: planning activities for long-term system maintenance and support.
Option C: final retirement and replacement of the current existing system.
Option D: final software deployment to the operational user community.
The provisional reviewed answer is A.
After identifying and analysing risks in a spiral iteration, development, or engineering, follows.
So in the Spiral model, risk analysis is not the end of the loop.
It informs what you build next, and the prototyping and engineering work comes straight after it.

Options B, C and D describe later or final lifecycle concerns, maintenance planning, retirement, and full deployment, none of which is the immediate next step after the risk assessment in a spiral iteration.
Now CA Question 9.
Arrange SDLC activities in logical progression starting from project initiation.
Which sequence best reflects standard SDLC flow?
Option A: planning, then analysis, then design, and finally coding.
Option B: coding, then testing, then planning, and finally analysis.
Option C: analysis, then deployment, then design, and finally maintenance.
Option D: design, then planning, then testing, and finally deployment.
The provisional reviewed answer is A.
Planning precedes requirement analysis, design, implementation and the later lifecycle phases.
Notice how the other options break the logic: B starts with coding before anything is planned or analysed, C deploys before designing, and D designs before planning.
Only A starts from initiation and moves forward in a sensible order.
Next, CA Question 13.
A vendor requires each development phase to be completed and formally approved before the next phase begins.
What model characteristic is described?
Option A: highly adaptive development cycles with constantly evolving priorities.
Option B: dynamic sprint-driven delivery using multiple small incremental releases.
Option C: sequential completion of clearly defined software development phases.
Option D: continuous customer feedback across various overlapping development phases.
The provisional reviewed answer is C.
The Waterfall model is sequential with clear phase exit criteria.
The key phrase in the stem is that each phase must be completed and formally approved before the next begins.
That is the exit-criteria idea.
Options A, B and D all describe the opposite temperament: adaptive priorities, sprints with small incremental releases, and overlapping phases with continuous feedback.
Now CA Question 20.
A university admission portal meets every documented requirement and acceptance criterion, but staff later discover approval workflows are missing.
What happened?
Option A: software specifications matched the documented requirements incorrectly.
Option B: system demonstrates poor maintainability rather than quality failure.
Option C: verification and validation processes failed the project completely.
Option D: verification succeeded while validation failed during the process.
The provisional reviewed answer is D.
Building according to the written specification differs from meeting real user and business needs.
This is the classic distinction between verification and validation.
Verification asks whether the product was built according to the specification, and here it was, because every documented requirement and acceptance criterion was met.
Validation asks whether the product meets the real needs of users and the business, and it did not, because the approval workflows staff needed were never captured.
So verification succeeded, while validation failed.
That is why option C, which says both failed completely, is too strong.
Then CA Question 21.
One student says SDLC is mainly programming; another says it integrates planning through maintenance.
Which understanding is more accurate?
Option A: SDLC applies only to large-scale enterprise software projects.
Option B: SDLC removes the need for verification and assurance.
Option C: SDLC focuses exclusively on coding and implementation tasks.
Option D: SDLC systematically integrates planning, development, testing, and maintenance.
The provisional reviewed answer is D.
Lifecycle management covers planning, requirements, design, implementation, testing, delivery and maintenance.
Programming is only one part of that whole.
Option C reduces the lifecycle to coding, option B wrongly claims SDLC removes verification and assurance, and option A restricts SDLC to large enterprise projects, which the source does not support.
Finally, the heading CA Question 29.

In the material supplied here, this heading appears without any question text, options, answer or reasoning following it, so there is nothing further for me to teach under it, and I will not invent a stem or answer for it.
